chunks: Ali ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Abi Abdullah, from Isḥāq ibn Muḥammad al-Nakhāʾī, who said:

Al-Fahfakī asked Abū Muḥammad (peace be upon him): 'What is the matter that the poor, weak woman takes one share, while the man takes two shares?' So Abū Muḥammad (peace be upon him) said: 'Indeed, upon the woman there is no Jiḥād, nor Nafaqah (maintenance expenses), nor Maʿqilah (bride price/dowry payment), but rather that is upon the men.'

So I said to myself: 'It was said to me that Ibn Abī al-ʿAwjāʾ asked Abū ʿAbdillāh (peace be upon him) about this issue, and he answered him with this answer.' So Abū Muḥammad (peace be upon him) turned to me and said: 'Yes, this is the issue of Ibn Abī al-ʿAwjāʾ, and the answer from us is one. When the meaning of the issue is one, what happened to our last one [Imam] happened to our first one [Imam], and our first one and our last one are equal in Knowledge, and for the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) and the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) is their preference.'

key_terms.أَوَّلُنَا وَآخِرُنَا: Our first one and our last one (referring to the Imams)
key_terms.ابْنُ أَبِي الْعَوْجَاءِ: Ibn Abī al-ʿAwjāʾ (a companion who asked the question)
key_terms.جِهَادٌ: Jihad (striving), here referring to financial expenditure for war

ai.seo_question: Why do men receive double the inheritance share of women in Islam according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Kafi elucidates the wisdom behind the 2:1 inheritance ratio by linking it to the principle of financial equity, noting that women are exempt from the burdens of Jihad, Nafaqah, and Ma'qilah which fall upon men. It further emphasizes the doctrinal continuity of the Ahl al-Bayt, illustrating that the Imams' rulings remain consistent across generations as long as the underlying meaning remains unchanged. This context reinforces the Shia view of inheritance not as arbitrary preference but as a balanced distribution of fiscal responsibilities within the family structure.
